Uzbekistan’s Electric Utilities Grapple with Widening Debt Crisis

Uzbekistan’s electric utilities sector is facing mounting turmoil as a deepening debt crisis strains the industry’s stability, according to sector participants and regulators. The crisis, which began to unfold in late May, was triggered by a sudden freeze in credit facilities extended by major domestic banks to power generation and grid companies. As a result, several utilities, including Tashkent Energo and Zarafshan Electric, have reported difficulties in servicing existing debt and maintaining operating cash flow.

According to the Uzbekistan Association of Grid Operators, outstanding short-term liabilities for the sector have surged by 38% year-on-year, reaching an estimated 2.6 trillion som as of June 10. “Credit lines that were once routinely rolled over have been abruptly suspended,” said Timur Sabirov, the association’s spokesperson. “Many of our members are now struggling to make scheduled payments to suppliers and to finance essential maintenance work.”

The Ministry of Energy has acknowledged the crisis, warning in a statement on Tuesday that “continued disruption to financing could undermine the reliability of electricity supply and delay critical network upgrades.” The ministry is reportedly in talks with commercial banks and the central bank to explore emergency liquidity support.

Industry analysts caution that the situation remains fluid. Gulnara Yuldasheva, an independent sector analyst, noted that wholesale electricity prices have declined by nearly 15% since early May, further eroding revenues. “Utilities are caught in a vicious cycle: lower prices and frozen credit are squeezing working capital, just as summer demand peaks,” she said.

Union representatives for utility workers have also voiced concerns over job security. “Staff reductions are already being discussed at several companies,” said Mukhtar Rakhimov, head of the National Utility Workers’ Council. “We urge all stakeholders to find a solution before operations are compromised further.”

The crisis remains unresolved as negotiations continue.
